messages.subject_clean: Software Carpentry Workshop at Chico State Aug 13-14
messages.body_plain:
Hi D-Ruggies,

I know that there is a lot of Software & Data Carpentry training going on at Davis, but I would like to share our workshop in case anyone is interested.

On August 13 - 15th, the Data Science Initiative at Chico State is hosting a Software Carpentry workshop for graduate students, faculty, and any other researcher that wants to learn how to conduct reproducible research. You don’t need to have any previous knowledge of the tools that will be presented at the workshop

This workshop is focused on Reproducible Scientific research using R. The curriculum will include:
Day 1: Monday August 13, 9am - 4:30 pm
Organizing data in spreadsheets
Getting started with R and Markdown
Day 2: Tuesday August 14, 9am - 4:30 pm
Command line power: using the shell
Data visualization and manipulation
Day 3: (optional) Wednesday August 13, 9am - 12 noon
Version control in R Studio using Projects
Building websites in R with Markdown

The target audience is learners who have little to no prior computational experience, and the instructors put a priority on creating a friendly environment to empower researchers and enable data-driven discovery. Even those with some experience will benefit, as the goal is to teach not only how to do analyses, but how to manage the process to make it as automated and reproducible as possible. For instance, after attending this workshop you will be able to:
Use the unix shell to manage files without a graphical user interface.
Import, process and visualize data sets in R Studio
Create reproducible scientific documents that are human readable.
(Optional) Build a website where you can share research, post course materials, or start an e-portfolio to demonstrate your work.

See the workshop website <http://bit.ly/2mzF9FD> for specific details on the topics, schedule and RSVP instructions.  https://csucdsi.github.io/2018-08-13-chicostate/

Contact Robin at datas...@csuchico.edu if you have any questions.

messages.subject_clean: Model structure and subsamples to avoid pseudoreplication
messages.body_plain:
Hi all! I am working with some count data, and we want to analyze these data to determine if there is a difference in counts between PlotTypes. I am running into an issue where my coding clearly is not picking up the fact that Image is a subsample, and not a replicate, and it is definitely causing issues (I would assume I am pseudoreplicating). I don't quite know what I need to do, and after two weeks of searching and trying, am still stuck. Here is the design that we have:
Subarea = 3 Subareas (these are the sites, a random factor)
PlotID = Varying numbers of plots within each subarea (varies by subarea, should be nested in subarea) - 1 camera per plot, so really Plot represents the same thing as camera, and I am using PlotID as the predictor. Each plot, regardless of subarea, has a unique identifier.
Year * = 2 years
SamplePer * = 6 Sample Periods per Year; each sample period is a six-day period from which 10 wildlife camera images were randomly selected per treatment level). Sample Periods are the same for all subareas and plots.
Image = ~10 (sometimes more, sometimes less) randomly selected images from each day within the six-day period of each SamplePer. The response is a count. We cannot average across these images to get an average "count" because not all of the predictors for each image are continuous; some are categorical, and we can't average across those predictors to get average predictor values to accompany each response value. Image numbers are all over the place; no rhyme or reason to them; maybe they are all unique, maybe not; likely not; but unlikely to have a same sample period, plot, year, etc, that all share the same image number for what are actually different images. I assume this is a random term that needs to be in the model.
PlotType = 2 main treatment types (Control vs. Trt); there are varying numbers of control vs. trt plots within each subarea, depending on what was available to work with. Not randomly selected, because had to be a certain size, and the "treatment" is just the condition that happens to be in place there.
Other Predictors: There are three others (categorical and continuous). The categorical ones are not fully crossed with the plot type.
Some Notes:
- Subareas are blocks, and plots are replicates.
- Year and SamplePer make this repeated measures, because the sampling occurs on the same plots each sampler period and year, and the treatment doesn't change (at least for these plots).
- The responses are are massively zero-inflated and over-dispersed.
- I am using glmmADMB tto start, family poisson (or negative binomial). Will be looking at hurdle models too, and glmmTMB. But the actual model specification is PRIORITY NUMBER ONE!

Now the model: fit_zipoiss2 <- glmmadmb(Count ~ PlotType + Year/SamplePer + TS + WD + OW + (1|Subarea) + (1|PlotID/Image) , data=data, zeroInflation=TRUE, family="poisson")

I would really love some feedback or tips to ensure I do not pseudoreplicate. Thank you so much in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Hi friends,

I'm new to vegan/community analyses, and could use some help with making rarefaction curves.

Basically, I have a dataset that consists of 98 10-min audio samples taken at 10 different lakesides. For each clip, I manually identified every sound present. I filtered the results to bird species only, so each sample represents a 10-minute auditory survey of the avian community. I have 2 community matrices: one that is populated by the number of calls per species, and another that I've coerced to incidence only (0/1) data. It's a lil sketchy to use the call# data (because it doesn't reaaaaally reliably mean anything about abundance), but I included it anyway.

I also have a corresponding environmental matrix that describes some relevant covariates (elevation, treatment/control, etc).

Comm = the community matrix with call #
pa = the community matrix with cells coerced to presence/absence (1/0)
Comm.env = corresponding environmental covariates

I made species accumulation curves, which indicate to me that the number of samples per lake I took isn't enough to describe the entire community actually present at each lake.

Furthermore, my sample size (# of audio recordings) varies by lake, so

I'd like to make some rarefaction curves so that I can report rarefied species richness for each lake (rarefied to the lake with the smallest # of surveys (7)).

I think in order to do this, I'll need to subset my matrix by lake, and calculate a separate curve for each (?). But first, I just wanted to see if I could make one on the entire dataset.

> S <- specnumber(pa) # observed number of species
> (raremax <- min(rowSums(pa)))
[1] 1
> Srare <- rarefy(pa, 1) # rarefied number of species
> rarecurve(pa, step = 1, sample = raremax, col = divmatrix.env$fish, cex = 0.6)
Error in approx(x = attr(z, "Subsample"), y = z, xout = sample, rule = 1) :
  need at least two non-NA values to interpolate
>

Could it be that the couple of recordings that have only 1 species present is screwing this up somehow?

I've attached the two matrices and the relevant code.

Any help very much appreciated! Thanks, D-RUG!

More on the study design:
The 10 lakes are in pairs of "fish-containing" and "fishless", each pair is nested within a unique basin. So, 5 basins, 10 lakes, 1 "treatment" (fish-containing) and 1 control (fishless).
Lakes vary in elevation and size. Those data reside in divmatrix.env
A few of the recordings are VERY sparse in vocal activity, with only 1 species calling.
This is a random sample of recordings from a much larger dataset; these recordings were taken in a 5-day period in late breeding season (8-12 July 2015).

Hi Mary,

I think you're correct that a "raremax" value of 1 is returning a strange result for your rarefaction curves - the rarefy() and rarecurve() functions in vegan conduct individual-based rarefaction, so if you specify a raremax value of 1, you will only ever get a single species. As an aside, if you're not sure about individual abundances, I think you may want to stick with sample-based rarefaction (specaccum()), which it looks like you were using beforehand.

If I understand your study design correctly, I agree that you need aggregate your data by lakes so that each row contains the sum of all the individual counts for that site. To run the rarefy() function for the entire dataset, you can sum your species counts and run the code as before - the rarecurve function operates on a single row of a matrix.

# Aggregating dataset
comm_agg = colSums(pa) # summing species counts by column
S <- specnumber(comm_agg) # observed number of species
raremax = 20 # number of individuals to use in rarefaction

# Plotting rarefied species number
Srare <- rarefy(comm_agg, raremax) # rarefied number of species
plot(S, Srare, xlab = "Observed No. of Species", ylab = "Rarefied No. of Species")
abline(0, 1)

# Plotting rarefaction curve
rarecurve(matrix(comm_agg, nrow = 1), step = 1, sample = raremax, cex = 0.6)

I get this as the output:

I've also attached code to do the same for site-level rarefaction.

Hope this helps!

-Evan

I’m using R to clean up an old dataset and have figured out numerous errors in the originally inputted species codes that I would like to fix.

I’ve worked out one way to do this, with a function that deals with each error one at a time (using gsub to find all instances of a single offending string and replace it with the correct one). This example function takes in a dataframe, where my column of interest is “veg.species”, incorrect values to replace are “POAPRA” “RHAILL” and “CARPYN” with each one getting replaced by “POASEC” “RHAILI” and “CARPYC”, respectively.

CleanSpecies <- function(df){
  df$veg.species <- gsub("POAPRA","POASEC", df$veg.species)
  df$veg.species <- gsub("RHAILL","RHAILI", df$veg.species)
  df$veg.species <- gsub("CARPYN","CARPYC", df$veg.species)
.
.
.
  return(df)
}

However, with 20+ errors to fix, this is an ugly chunk of code. Is there a way to do this by providing paired vectors of the original inputs and cleaned outputs? I’ve tried searching online but haven’t had any luck.

Thanks!
Chhaya

~
Chhaya M. Werner
PhD Candidate, Population Biology
University of California Davis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chhaya,

I would consider doing this is by creating a lookup table (just a CSV file) of your old species name inputs and the new cleaned outputs you want. This would essentially be the paired vectors strategy you're talking about. So basically, create that lookup table outside of R as a CSV (or XLS or whatever you want) and import it into your R session.

lookup <- read.csv("my_lookup_table.csv")

Let's assume the two columns in the lookup table are "veg.species.original" and "veg.species.cleaned". So now you can simply join your lookup table to your existing dataframe.

df <- left_join(df, lookup, by = c("veg.species" = "veg.species.original"))

You've told R that df$veg.species should have some matching values in lookup$veg.species.original, and you'll create a new "veg.species.cleaned" column in your df. Now you can simply fill out the remainder of "veg.species.cleaned" with the original, good species name values (i.e., the ones that didn't need to be changed).

df$veg.species.cleaned <- ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(df$veg.species.cleaned), df$veg.species, df$veg.species.cleaned)

So anywhere there's a missing "veg.species.cleaned" value (because it didn't need to be replaced), you want the original "veg.species" value, and if there's already a "veg.species.cleaned" value, you keep it.

There are certainly other ways to do this. I really like the function case_when() but it essentially does what you were already doing, I just find it clean and flexible. To me, the approach I just outlined has a few benefits though:

1) I find it way easier to input and look at this type of original/corrected name data in Excel rather than R.
2) You actually keep your original species names in your dataframe as well as creating a new modified, species name column. Sure, it's redundant, but it can also help you verify the changes that got made are the changes you wanted.
3) The lookup table workflow is easily modified. Say you discover another species name needs to be cleaned up. Just add the original and cleaned entries into a new row of your CSV, rerun those lines of code, and you're good to go.

Hope that helps,
Evan

messages.body_plain:
Great suggestions! One added one I've used a lot recently for this sort of thing, it's flexible and you can add multiple searches within a single line which is also nice: case_when <https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/case_when.html> from dplyr. You can either overwrite an existing column, or create a new one with the "cleaned" version to make sure it works as you wanted (as below).

Using your example:

df <- df %>%
  mutate(veg.species.cleaned = case_when(
    grepl("POAPRA", veg.species) ~ "POASEC",
    grepl("RHAILL", veg.species) ~ "RHAILI",
    grepl("CARPYN|CARPIN|CRPYN", veg.species) ~ "CARPYC", # for multiple searches
    TRUE ~ veg.species))

Hope this helps,

Adios,
Ryan

HTH,
B

)

output = list(list(9,5,5), list(80,5,15), list(65,10,25), list(20,65,15), list(40,20,40))
)

iter_func <-
function(df, iter) {
df %>%
mutate(row_num = row_number()) %>%
gather(., key, value, -row_num) %>%
full_join(., trans_table, by = c("value" = "symb")) %>%
mutate(output = map_dbl(output, ~pluck(., iter))) %>%
select(-value) %>%
spread(., key, output) %>%
select(-row_num)
}

iter_vec <- c(1,2,3)

map(iter_vec, ~ iter_func(char_df, .))

HTH,
B

char_df is the character table that needs translating. I'm sorry I didn't comment the code much. It was late for me and once I cracked it, I needed to go.

You should be able to replace char_df for your table, but your table is kind of messy.

You have two header rows. You have empty columns. The function does not expect any other columns.

Additionally, your original translation will not work because S, IL, SC and so on are not the way your soil types are represented in your actual dataset.

You need to edit a few things, but here is it working on your dataset:

library(tidyverse)

char_df <-
read_csv("~/Downloads/profile for r.csv", skip =1) %>% # reads in file, skips first row
select(-starts_with("X")) #removes blank columns

legend <- select(char_df, 1:2) # holds back variables that don't need translating

char_df2 <- select(char_df, 3:ncol(char_df)) #gets rid of extra variables

# this is your translation table. You need to fix these values
# because your example did not match your real data
trans_table <-
tibble(
symb = c("sand","siC", "sL", "clay", "loam", "cL*"),
output = list(list(9,5,5), list(80,5,15), list(65,10,25), list(20,65,15), list(40,20,40), list(25,25,25))
)

# this function does all the work
iter_func <-
function(df, iter) { #takes a data.frame/tibble and a number to pull from
df %>%
mutate(row_num = row_number()) %>% #add row numbers for later spreading
gather(., key, value, -row_num) %>% #gather everything up in long form
full_join(., trans_table, by = c("value" = "symb")) %>% #join the translation table to convert to  alues
mutate(output = map_dbl(output, ~pluck(., iter, .default = NA_real_))) %>% # iterate over all of the values in main column and pull out the [iter]th value
# needed to change the default output to NA_real_ so that map_dbl wouldn't complain about NULL not being an atomic vector
select(-value) %>% #remove the original code
spread(., key, output) %>% #spread it back out as it was
select(-row_num) %>% #get rid of the row number IDs
bind_cols(legend, .) #bind the legnd columns back out
}

iter_vec <- c(1,2,3) # we want to iterate over the three layers

map(iter_vec, ~ iter_func(char_df2, .)) #lets map over the iter_vec and pull out a dataframe at a time.

# returns a list with three dataframes in it.

Got it.

This was happening because I was doing a full_join of the translation table and the data. This was incorrect because it leaves unused translations at the bottom. These have NA values for position (row_number) and spread doesn't like that. Changed it to a left_join() which only pulls translations from things that exist in your data.

Try this and I hope it works.

B

read_csv("~/Downloads/profile for r.csv", skip =1) %>% # reads in file, skips first row
select(-starts_with("X")) #removes blank columns

legend <- select(char_df, 1:2) # holds back variables that don't need translating

# this is your translation table. You need to fix these values
# because your example did not match your real data

output = list(list(9,5,5), list(80,5,15), list(65,10,25), list(20,65,15), list(40,20,40), list(25,25,25))
)
